[[File:Pedal circle 4 points.svg|thumb|upright=1.4|4 points <math>A,B,C,D</math> and 4 pedal circles intersecting in <math>S</math>]]

The '''pedal circle''' of the a triangle <math>ABC</math> and a point <math>P</math> in the plane is a special circle determined by those two entities. More specifically for the three perpendiculars through the point <math> P</math> onto the three (extended) triangle sides <math> a,b,c</math> you get three points of intersection <math>P_a, P_b, P_c</math> and the circle defined by those three points is the pedal circle. By definition the pedal circle is the [[circumcircle]] of the [[pedal triangle]].<ref name ="Honsberger">[[Ross Honsberger]]: ''Episodes in Nineteenth and Twentieth Century Euclidean Geometry''. MAA, 1995, pp. 67–75</ref><ref name="Johnson">Roger A. Johnson: Advanced Euclidean Geometry. Dover 2007 (reprint), ISBN 978-0-486-46237-0, pp. 135–144, 155, 240</ref>

For radius <math>r</math> of the pedal circle the following formula holds with <math>R</math> being the radius and <math>O</math> being the center of the circumcircle:<ref name="Johnson"/>
:<math>r=\frac{|PA| \cdot |PB| \cdot |PC|}{2\cdot (R^2-|PO|^2)} </math>
Note that the denominator in the formula turns 0 if the point <math>P</math> lies on the circumcircle. In this case the three points  <math>P_a, P_b, P_c </math> determine a degenerated circle with an infinite radius, that is a line. This is the [[Simson line]]. If <math>P</math> is the [[incenter]] of the triangle then the pedal circle is the [[incircle]] of the triangle and if <math>P</math> is the [[orthocenter]] of the triangle the pedal circle is the [[nine-point circle]].<ref name="mw">{{MathWorld|title=Pedal Circle|urlname=PedalCircle}}</ref>

If <math>P</math> does not lie on the circumcircle then its [[isogonal conjugate]] <math>Q</math> yields the same pedal circle, that is the six points  <math>P_a, P_b, P_c </math> and  <math>Q_a, Q_b, Q_c </math> lie on the same circle. Moreover, the [[midpoint]] of the line segment <math>PQ</math> is the center of that pedal circle.<ref name ="Honsberger"/>

[[Griffiths' theorem]] states that all the pedal circles for points located on a line through the center of the triangle's circumcircle share a common (fixed) point.<ref>{{MathWorld|title=Griffiths' Theorem|urlname=GriffithsTheorem}}</ref>

Consider four points with no three of them being on a common line. Then you can build four different subsets of three points. Take the points of such a subset as the vertices of a triangle <math>ABC</math> and the fourth point as the point <math>P</math>, then they define a pedal circle. The four pedal circles you get this way intersect in a [[Poncelet point|common point]].<ref name="mw"/>
